lead: An encoder-decoder model turns one sequence into another sequence of a different length. The encoder reads the source and compresses it into a context vector c. The decoder starts from c and generates the target one token at a time, feeding each produced token back as the next input. This design powers translation, speech-to-text, summarisation and image captioning. It exists because plain RNNs predict same-length tags or next tokens, while many tasks need a full source sentence read before a full target sentence is written. Some syllabi call it seq2seq or sequence-to-sequence.
prereq: You need: 4.2 for RNN cells and 4.1 for sequence tasks.

blocks.text: A sequence-to-sequence task maps a source sequence x₁ … xT to a target sequence y₁ … yU. Lengths T and U can differ. Translation is the standard case: an English sentence of 7 words can become a Tamil sentence of 9 words. A same-length tagger from 4.1 does not need this split.

The encoder is an RNN, often an LSTM from 4.4. It reads x₁ … xT in order. Its final hidden state hT becomes the context vector c. Some models use a small summary network on hT, but the basic idea is one fixed-size vector.
P(y₁ … y<sub>U</sub> | x₁ … x<sub>T</sub>) = Π<sub>t=1</sub><sup>U</sup> P(y<sub>t</sub> | y₁ … y<sub>t−1</sub>, c)
blocks.where: c is the encoder context vector; y<sub>t</sub> is the target token at step t; y₁ … y<sub>t−1</sub> are earlier target tokens; P(y<sub>t</sub> | ...) is the decoder softmax probability for token y<sub>t</sub>.

blocks.text: The decoder is a second RNN. It starts with c and a start token. At step t it takes the previous target token and the previous decoder state. It outputs logits z<sub>t</sub> over the vocabulary. Softmax turns z<sub>t</sub> into probabilities. The model either picks the highest-probability token or samples.

The fixed vector c is a bottleneck. Every detail of the source must pass through the same c. Long source sentences lose information. The symptom is that translation quality drops as input length grows. Attention in Unit 5 lets the decoder look back at all encoder states instead of only c.

Training uses pairs of source and target sequences. At decoder step t, the correct previous target y<sub>t−1</sub> is fed as input. This is teacher forcing. The decoder never sees its own wrong guess during training, so gradients are stable.
L = −Σ<sub>t=1</sub><sup>U</sup> log P(y<sub>t</sub> = true token | y₁ … y<sub>t−1</sub>, c)
blocks.where: L is the total cross-entropy loss over the target sequence; log is natural log; true token is the target token at step t.

blocks.text: Backpropagation through time from 4.3 flows through decoder and encoder. The encoder learns a c that helps the decoder.

Teacher forcing creates a mismatch. At inference the true previous token is not available, so the decoder must use its own previous output. A small early error then changes later inputs. Scheduled sampling reduces this: with probability ε feed the true token, with probability 1−ε feed the model's token. ε is often decreased over training.

items: Training input at step t: true y<sub>t−1</sub>.
Inference input at step t: predicted previous token.
Never mix the two unless scheduled sampling is explicit.

blocks.text: Inference starts with c and a start token. Greedy decoding picks the token with the largest probability at each step, appends it, and feeds it back. It stops at an end token or at a maximum length. Greedy is fast but one bad early choice cannot be undone.

items: Set decoder state from c; input the start token.
Pick the argmax token; append it to the output.
If the token is an end token or the length limit is reached, stop; otherwise feed the token back.

blocks.text: Beam search keeps k partial sequences, called beams. Each beam has a score: the sum of log probabilities of its tokens. At each step expand every beam with all vocabulary tokens, keep the k highest scores, and continue. k is beam width. k = 1 is greedy. Beam search costs about k times more than greedy.
score(y₁ … y<sub>t</sub>) = Σ<sub>i=1</sub><sup>t</sup> log P(y<sub>i</sub> | y₁ … y<sub>i−1</sub>, c)
blocks.where: score is the log-probability of a partial output; log is natural log; a higher score means a more likely sequence.

blocks.text: Use greedy for quick demos and beam search when quality matters. Older RNN translation systems often used beam width 4 to 10. Length normalisation is needed because log probabilities are negative and longer sequences get lower scores; its variants are left to Unit 5.

figure.caption: The encoder compresses the source into one context vector c = [1, 0]; the decoder reads c and emits target tokens. Notice that the whole source passes through the single fixed vector.

spec.title: Seq2seq
spec.aria: Source tokens enter the encoder, become the context vector c = [1, 0], and the decoder emits target tokens from that vector.

examples.question: A toy seq2seq model has encoder context c = [1, 0]. The decoder vocabulary is {a, b, c, end}. At step 1 the decoder logits for a, b, c, end are [2, 1, 0, -1]. At step 2 the logits are [0, 1, 2, -1]. Use greedy decoding and stop after two tokens. Show the chosen token at each step and the final sequence as token indices (a = 0, b = 1, c = 2, end = 3).
steps: Step 1 logits: a = 2, b = 1, c = 0, end = −1. The largest is 2 at index 0, so the step-1 token is a.
Feed a back as the previous token. Step 2 logits: a = 0, b = 1, c = 2, end = −1. The largest is 2 at index 2, so the step-2 token is c.
Two tokens are produced, so stop. The output sequence is [a, c]; its token indices are [0, 2].
examples.answer: Greedy decoding outputs the token sequence [a, c], that is, token indices [0, 2].
examples.check:
step1 = [2, 1, 0, -1]
step2 = [0, 1, 2, -1]
i1 = max(range(len(step1)), key=lambda i: step1[i])
i2 = max(range(len(step2)), key=lambda i: step2[i])
print(i1)
print(i2)

code.code:
step1 = [2, 1, 0, -1]
step2 = [0, 1, 2, -1]
i1 = max(range(len(step1)), key=lambda i: step1[i])
i2 = max(range(len(step2)), key=lambda i: step2[i])
print(i1, i2)

traps: Feeding the true previous target token at inference is teacher forcing; a model trained that way but run without it must use its own previous output. Mixing the two in one decoding pass is a common exam error.
The basic encoder's context is the final hidden state h<sub>T</sub>, not the full list h₁ … h<sub>T</sub>. The full list is used by attention in Unit 5.
Do not call logits probabilities. Greedy argmax is the same on logits or softmax, but beam scores add log probabilities; applying softmax twice changes the values.
Input and output lengths need not match. Seq2seq supports T ≠ U; a same-length tagger does not.
The context c is a vector, not a single token or scalar; its size is fixed by the encoder hidden size.

quiz.q: What is the context vector in a basic encoder-decoder model?
quiz.a: The final hidden state h<sub>T</sub> of the encoder RNN, or a small summary of it. It is a fixed-size vector c that summarises the source sequence.

quiz.q: Why is teacher forcing used in seq2seq training?
quiz.a: It feeds the true previous target token at each decoder step, so the decoder is trained on correct prefixes and gradients are stable. It avoids early training on mostly wrong self-generated tokens.

quiz.q: Given c = [1, 0], step 1 logits [2, 1, 0, -1] and step 2 logits [0, 1, 2, -1] for tokens a, b, c, end, what does greedy decoding output after two steps?
quiz.a: Step 1 argmax is a (index 0, score 2). Step 2 argmax is c (index 2, score 2). Output is [a, c], that is, token indices [0, 2].

quiz.q: Why does the fixed context vector hurt long source sentences? Name one symptom and one fix.
quiz.a: All source information must fit in one fixed-size c. Long sentences need more detail than c can hold, so translation quality drops as length grows. Attention lets the decoder read all encoder states, not just c.

quiz.q: State the difference between the decoder input at training and at inference in basic seq2seq.
quiz.a: Training uses the true previous target token, which is teacher forcing. Inference uses the model's own previous predicted token.

quiz.q: A beam width k = 2 decoder has first-step probabilities a = 0.6, b = 0.3, c = 0.1. Which beams survive after step 1?
quiz.a: Keep the two highest: a with score log 0.6 and b with score log 0.3. c is dropped.

quiz.q: Why can greedy decoding be worse than beam search?
quiz.a: Greedy commits to the highest-probability token at each step and cannot undo an early mistake. Beam search keeps k partial sequences, so a token with slightly lower first-step probability can still lead to a higher total log-probability sequence.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, seq2seq appears in speech recognition, machine translation, text summarisation and image captioning. Modern systems add attention and transformers, but the encoder-decoder split survives. Search next for teacher forcing, exposure bias, scheduled sampling and beam search. The fixed-vector bottleneck is the reason attention became standard.
